en.content:
Consider a unity-gain negative feedback system consisting of the plant G(s) (given below) and a proportional-integral controller. Let the proportional gain and integral gain be 3 and 1, respectively. For a unit step reference input, the final values of the controller output and the plant output, respectively, are

$$G(s) = {1 \over {s - 1}}$$
en.explanation:
Given system can be drawn as shown below,

Here,

$X(s) \rightarrow$ Controller output

$C(s) \rightarrow$ Plant output

$C(s)=R(s) \frac{\left(3+\frac{1}{s}\right)\left(\frac{1}{s-1}\right)}{1+\left(3+\frac{1}{s}\right) \frac{1}{s-1}}=R(s) \frac{(3 s+1)}{s(s-1)+3 s+1}=\frac{(3 s+1)}{s(s-1)+3 s+1} \times \frac{1}{s}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad c(\infty)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s C(s)=1 \\\\ & X(s)=[R(s)-C(s)]\left(3+\frac{1}{s}\right) \\\\ & X(s)=[R(s)-C(s)]\left(\frac{3 s+1}{s}\right) \\\\ & x(\infty)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s X(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0}[R(s)-C(s)](3 s+1)\end{aligned}$

$$ \begin{aligned} x(\infty) & =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s} \frac{(3 s+1)}{\left(s^2+2 s+1\right)}\right)(3 s+1) \\\\ & =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{s}\left[\frac{s^2+2 s+1-3 s-1}{s^2+2 s+1}\right](3 s+1) \\\\ & =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{s}\left[\frac{s^2-s}{s^2+2 s+1}\right](3 s+1)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{(s-1)(3 s+1)}{s^2+2 s+1}=-1 \end{aligned} $$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

en.content:
Consider a lead compensator of the form

$$K(s) = {{1 + {s \over a}} \over {1 + {s \over {\beta a}}}},\beta > 1,a > 0$$

The frequency at which this compensator produces maximum phase lead is 4 rad/s. At this frequency, the gain amplification provided by the controller, assuming asymptotic Bode-magnitude plot of $$K(s)$$, is 6 dB. The values of $$a,\beta$$, respectively, are
en.explanation:
Given the form of the lead compensator:

$ K(s) = \frac{1 + \frac{s}{a}}{1 + \frac{s}{\beta a}},\ \beta > 1,\ a > 0 $

At the frequency ω = 4 rad/s, this compensator produces the maximum phase lead, and the gain amplification provided by the controller, according to the asymptotic Bode-magnitude plot of $ K(s) $, is 6 dB. We need to find the values of $ a $ and $ \beta $.

Rewriting the given compensator:

$ K(s)=\frac{1 + \frac{s}{\alpha}}{1 + \frac{s}{\alpha \beta}} $

$ K(s)=\left(\frac{s + \alpha}{\alpha}\right) \times \left(\frac{\alpha \beta}{s + \alpha \beta}\right) $

$ K(s)=\frac{\beta(s + \alpha)}{s + \alpha \beta} $

$ \sqrt{\alpha \times \alpha \beta} = 4 $

This results in:

$ \alpha \sqrt{\beta} = 4 \ \text{..........(i)} $

Also:

$ \alpha \beta > \alpha \ \text{...........(ii)} $

Considering the magnitude of $ K(j \omega) $:

$ K(j \omega) = \frac{\beta(j \omega + \alpha)}{j \omega + \alpha \beta} $

$ |K(j \omega)| = \frac{\beta \sqrt{\omega^2 + \alpha^2}}{\sqrt{\omega^2 + (\alpha \beta)^2}} $

Given that at 4 rad/sec, the gain is 6 dB:

$ 20 \log_{10}|K(j \omega)| = 6 \ \text{dB} $

$ \Rightarrow |K(j \omega)| = 2 $

$ \Rightarrow \frac{\beta \sqrt{16 + \alpha^2}}{\sqrt{16 + (\alpha \beta)^2}} = 2 $

$ \Rightarrow \frac{\beta^2(16 + \alpha^2)}{16 + (\alpha \beta)^2} = 4 $

$ \Rightarrow \beta^2(16 + \alpha^2) = 64 + 4(\alpha \beta)^2 $

This simplifies to:

$ \alpha^2 \beta^2 + 16 \beta^2 = 64 + 4(\alpha \beta)^2 $

$ \Rightarrow 16 \beta^2 = 64 + 3(\alpha \beta)^2 $

By solving the above equations, it is found that only the values $ \alpha = 2 $ and $ \beta = 4 $ satisfy all the conditions (i), (ii), and (iii).

Thus, the correct values are $ a = 2 $ and $ \beta = 4 $.

Consider the state-space description of an LTI system with matrices

For the input, $$\sin (\omega t),\omega > 0$$, the value of $$\omega$$ for which the steady-state output of the system will be zero, is ___________ (Round off to the nearest integer).
en.explanation:
Given :

$A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], C=\left[\begin{array}{ll}3 & -2\end{array}\right]$ and $D=1$

Transfer function is given by,

$$ \begin{aligned} & T . F .=C[s I-A]^{-1} B+D \\\\ & {[s I-A]=\left[\begin{array}{cc} s & -1 \\ 1 & s+2 \end{array}\right]} \end{aligned} $$

$\begin{aligned} & {[s I-A]^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}s & -1 \\ 1 & s+2\end{array}\right]^{-1}} \\\\ & {[s I-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{s(s+2)+1}\left[\begin{array}{cc}s+2 & 1 \\ -1 & s\end{array}\right]}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & T . F .=\left[\begin{array}{ll}3 & -2\end{array}\right] \frac{1}{s(s+2)+1}\left[\begin{array}{cc}s+2 & 1 \\ -1 & s\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]+1 \\ & T . F .=\frac{1}{s^2+2 s+1}\left[\begin{array}{ll}3 & -2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}s+2 & 1 \\ -1 & s\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]+1 \\ & T . F .=\frac{1}{s^2+2 s+1}\left[\begin{array}{ll}3 & -2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ s\end{array}\right]+1\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \text { T.F. }=\frac{3-2 s}{s^2+2 s+1}+1 \\ & \text { T.F. }=\frac{s^2+4}{s^2+2 s+1} \\ & H(s)=\frac{s^2+4}{s^2+2 s+1} \\ & s=j \omega \\ & H(\mathrm{j} \omega)=\frac{4-\omega^2}{1+2 j \omega-\omega^2}\end{aligned}$

Steady state output of system is zero

$$ \begin{aligned} & 4-\omega^2=0 \\\\ & 4=\omega^2 \\\\ & \omega=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} $$

Hence, the correct answer is 2 .

en.explanation:
Let's analyze the operating modes of an induction machine and their corresponding slip ranges to determine the correct matching.

Slip (s) in an induction motor is defined as the difference between the synchronous speed ($$N_s$$) and the rotor speed ($$N_r$$), expressed as a fraction of the synchronous speed:

$$s = \frac{N_s - N_r}{N_s}$$

Understanding Slip Ranges:

  1. Running in Generator Mode: An induction machine acts as a generator when its rotor speed exceeds the synchronous speed ($$N_r > N_s$$). This means the slip is negative. In practical terms, the slip would be a fraction between 0.0 and -1.0 (excluding -1.0).
  2. Running in Motor Mode: A standard induction motor operation occurs when the rotor speed is less than the synchronous speed ($$N_r < N_s$$). This results in a positive slip, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0 (excluding 1.0).
  3. Plugging in Motor Mode: This mode involves reversing the direction of the rotor's magnetic field. The motor is brought to a sudden stop and then reversed. The slip here is greater than 1, potentially reaching values up to 2.0.

Correct Matching:

Based on our understanding of slip ranges:

  • a - r: Running in generator mode corresponds to a slip range of from -1.0 to 0.0.
  • b - p: Running in motor mode corresponds to a slip range of from 0.0 to 1.0.
  • c - q: Plugging in motor mode corresponds to a slip range of from 1.0 to 2.0.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option A: a-r, b-p, and c-q.

en.content: A 10-pole, 50 Hz, 240 V, single phase induction motor runs at 540 RPM while driving rated load. The frequency of induced rotor currents due to backward field is
en.explanation:
To determine the frequency of the induced rotor currents due to the backward field, we first need to understand a few key concepts about induction motors and their operation under load conditions.

The synchronous speed (ns) of an induction motor is given by the formula:

$$ n_s = \frac{120 \cdot f}{P} $$

where:

  • ns = Synchronous speed in revolutions per minute (RPM)
  • f = Supply frequency in Hertz (Hz)
  • P = Number of poles

For a 10-pole motor running at a supply frequency of 50 Hz, the synchronous speed can be calculated as follows:

$$ n_s = \frac{120 \cdot 50}{10} = 600 \, \text{RPM} $$

The motor operates at 540 RPM, which is slightly less than the synchronous speed due to slip. Slip (s) is given by the formula:

$$ s = \frac{n_s - n_r}{n_s} $$

where:

  • nr = Rotor speed in RPM

Plugging in the known values:

$$ s = \frac{600 - 540}{600} = \frac{60}{600} = 0.1 $$

The slip (s) is 0.1 or 10%. The frequency of the rotor currents in the forward field can be calculated as:

$$ f_r = s \cdot f $$

Substituting the values, we get:

$$ f_r = 0.1 \cdot 50 = 5 \, \text{Hz} $$

However, for the backward rotating field, the rotor currents operate at a slip of (2-s) with respect to the stator frequency. Thus, the frequency of induced rotor current due to the backward field can be calculated as follows:

$$ f_{b} = (2 - s) \cdot f $$

Substituting the known values, we get:

$$ f_{b} = (2 - 0.1) \cdot 50 = 1.9 \cdot 50 = 95 \, \text{Hz} $$

Therefore, the frequency of the induced rotor currents due to the backward field is 95 Hz. So, the correct answer is:

Option B: 95 Hz

en.content: A separately excited DC motor rated 400 V, 15 A, 1500 RPM drives a constant torque load at rated speed operating from 400 V DC supply drawing rated current. The armature resistance is 1.2 $$\Omega$$. If the supply voltage drops by 10% with field current unaltered then the resultant speed of the motor in RPM is ____________ (Round off to the nearest integer).
en.explanation:
To find the resultant speed of the motor, we need to first understand the relationship between the supply voltage, back EMF, and speed of the motor. We will use the following equations for a DC motor:

1. The back EMF equation:

$$E_b = V - I_a R_a$$

where:

$$E_b$$ is the back EMF

$$V$$ is the supply voltage

$$I_a$$ is the armature current

$$R_a$$ is the armature resistance

2. The relationship between back EMF and speed:

$$E_b \propto \phi n$$

where:

$$\phi$$ is the flux (which is proportional to the field current and assumed to be constant)

$$n$$ is the speed in RPM

Given data:

Supply voltage, $$V = 400 \, V$$

Armature current, $$I_a = 15 \, A$$

Armature resistance, $$R_a = 1.2 \, \Omega$$

Rated speed, $$n = 1500 \, RPM$$

First, let's calculate the back EMF at rated condition:

$$E_{b_{\text{rated}}} = V - I_a R_a = 400 \, V - 15 \, A \times 1.2 \, \Omega = 400 - 18 = 382 \, V$$

If the supply voltage drops by 10%, the new supply voltage is:

$$V_{\text{new}} = 0.9 \times 400 \, V = 360 \, V$$

With the new supply voltage, the new back EMF can be calculated as:

$$E_{b_{\text{new}}} = V_{\text{new}} - I_a R_a = 360 \, V - 15 \, A \times 1.2 \, \Omega = 360 - 18 = 342 \, V$$

Since the flux $$\phi$$ is constant, the back EMF is directly proportional to the speed of the motor:

$$\frac{E_{b_{\text{new}}}}{E_{b_{\text{rated}}}} = \frac{n_{\text{new}}}{n_{\text{rated}}}$$

Rearranging to find the new speed:

$$n_{\text{new}} = n_{\text{rated}} \times \frac{E_{b_{\text{new}}}}{E_{b_{\text{rated}}}} = 1500 \, RPM \times \frac{342 \, V}{382 \, V}$$

$$n_{\text{new}} \approx 1500 \times 0.895 = 1343 \, RPM$$

Therefore, the resultant speed of the motor when the supply voltage drops by 10%, with the field current unaltered, is approximately 1343 RPM.

A quadratic function of two variables is given as

$$f({x_1},{x_2}) = x_1^2 + 2x_2^2 + 3{x_1} + 3{x_2} + {x_1}{x_2} + 1$$

The magnitude of the maximum rate of change of the function at the point (1, 1) is ___________ (Round off to the nearest integer).
en.explanation:
To find the magnitude of the maximum rate of change of the given function at the point $(1, 1)$, we need to compute the gradient of the function. The gradient vector represents the direction and rate of the steepest ascent.

The given quadratic function is:

$$f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 + 2x_2^2 + 3x_1 + 3x_2 + x_1 x_2 + 1$$

The gradient vector $\nabla f$ is calculated by finding the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x_1$ and $x_2$.

First, compute the partial derivative with respect to $x_1$:

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} \left( x_1^2 + 2 x_2^2 + 3 x_1 + 3 x_2 + x_1 x_2 + 1 \right)$$

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = 2 x_1 + 3 + x_2$$

Next, compute the partial derivative with respect to $x_2$:

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} \left( x_1^2 + 2 x_2^2 + 3 x_1 + 3 x_2 + x_1 x_2 + 1 \right)$$

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = 4 x_2 + 3 + x_1$$

Now, evaluate the gradient vector at the point $(1, 1)$:

$$\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \right|_{(1,1)} = 2(1) + 3 + 1 = 6$$

$$\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \right|_{(1,1)} = 4(1) + 3 + 1 = 8$$

So, the gradient vector at point $(1, 1)$ is:

$$\nabla f(1, 1) = (6, 8)$$

The magnitude of the gradient vector is given by the Euclidean norm:

$$|\nabla f(1, 1)| = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10$$

Therefore, the magnitude of the maximum rate of change of the function at the point $(1, 1)$ is 10.

Consider the following equation in a 2-D real-space.

$$|{x_1}{|^p} + |{x_2}{|^p} = 1$$ for $$p > 0$$

Which of the following statement(s) is/are true.

options.content: When p = 2, the area enclosed by the curve is $$\pi$$.
When p tends to $$\infty$$, the area enclosed by the curve tends to 4.
When p tends to 0, the area enclosed by the curve is 1.
When p = 1, the area enclosed by the curve is 2.

en.explanation:
Let's analyze each of the options given for the equation:

$$|x_1|^p + |x_2|^p = 1$$

where $$p > 0$$.

Option A: When $$p = 2$$, the area enclosed by the curve is $$\pi$$.

When $$p=2$$, the equation becomes:

$$x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1$$

This represents a circle with radius 1. The area of a circle is given by $$\pi r^2$$. For a radius of 1, the area is:

$$\pi \times 1^2 = \pi$$

So, Option A is true.

Option B: When $$p$$ tends to $$\infty$$, the area enclosed by the curve tends to 4.

As $$p \to \infty$$, the equation describes a shape that approaches a square with vertices at (1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), and (0,-1). The side length of this square is 2, and the area of the square is:

$$2 \times 2 = 4$$

So, Option B is true.

Option C: When $$p$$ tends to 0, the area enclosed by the curve is 1.

If we examine the behavior as $$p \to 0$$, the points satisfying the equation $$|x_1|^p + |x_2|^p = 1$$ tend to lie close to the coordinate axes. It does not cover a finite area, rather it tends to cover the entire plane except along the axes. Therefore, this statement is false.

Option D: When $$p = 1$$, the area enclosed by the curve is 2.

For $$p=1$$, the equation becomes:

$$|x_1| + |x_2| = 1$$

This represents a diamond (or a square rotated by 45 degrees) with vertices at (1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), and (0,-1). The area of this diamond-shaped figure is given by the formula for the area of a square with side length $$\sqrt{2}$$:

$$\left(\frac{\text{diagonal}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \left( \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^2 \times \left( \sqrt{2} \right)^2 = 2$$

Hence, Option D is true.

So, the correct answers are:

  • Option A
  • Option B
  • Option D

en.content: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is __________ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
en.explanation:
The problem describes a biased coin where the expected number of trials for the first occurrence of a "head" is 4. Let's denote the probability of getting a head by $ p $ and thus the probability of getting a tail by $ 1 - p $.

We know that if the expected number of trials to get a head is 4, then:

$$ E(X) = \frac{1}{p} $$

Given that $ E(X) = 4 $, we have:

$$ 4 = \frac{1}{p} $$

Solving for $ p $, we get:

$$ p = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25 $$

Now, we need to find the probability of getting the first head in the second trial. This means the first trial is a tail, and the second trial is a head. The probability of this event is:

$$ P(\text{first occurrence of head in second trial}) = (1 - p) \times p $$

$$ = (1 - 0.25) \times 0.25 $$

$$ = 0.75 \times 0.25 $$

$$ = 0.1875 $$

Rounding this to three decimal places, the probability is 0.188.

Therefore, the probability of the first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is 0.188.

en.content: Given a fair six-faced dice where the faces are labelled '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', and '6', what is the probability of getting a '1' on the first roll of the dice and a '4' on the second roll?
en.explanation:
Since the dice is fair, all the six faces have an equal probability of appearing on each roll. The probability of getting a '1' on the first roll is 1/6, and the probability of getting a '4' on the second roll is also $${1 \over 6}$$.

Since the two rolls are independent of each other, meaning that the outcome of one roll does not affect the outcome of the other roll, we can find the probability of both events happening together by multiplying their individual probabilities :

Probability of getting a '1' on the first roll and a '4' on the second roll

= Probability of getting a '1' on the first roll $$ \times $$ Probability of getting a '4' on the second roll

= $${1 \over 6}$$ $$ \times $$ $${1 \over 6}$$

= $${1 \over {36}}$$

Therefore, the probability of getting a '1' on the first roll of the dice and a '4' on the second roll is $${1 \over {36}}$$.

en.content: the digit in the unit's place of the product $$3^{999}\times7^{1000}$$ is __________.
en.explanation:
To find the unit digit of the given product, we only need to consider the unit digit of each factor, because the other digits will not affect the unit digit of the product.

Let's analyze the unit digits of the two factors separately :

The units digit of $3^n$ has a repeating cycle of 4: 3, 9, 7, 1, 3, 9, 7, 1, ...

The units digit of $7^n$ has a repeating cycle of 4: 7, 9, 3, 1, 7, 9, 3, 1, ...

For powers of 3, the unit's digit follows the cycle: 3, 9, 7, 1. So, the unit's digit of $3^{999}$ will be the same as that of $3^{999\mod 4}$, which is $3^3 = 27$, and hence the unit's digit is 7.

For powers of 7, the unit's digit follows the cycle: 7, 9, 3, 1. So, the unit's digit of $7^{1000}$ will be the same as that of $7^{1000\mod 4}$, which is $7^0 = 1$, and hence the unit's digit is 1.

Multiplying the unit's digits of $3^{999}$ and $7^{1000}$ gives us $7\times 1 = 7$.

Therefore, the digit in the unit's place of the product $3^{999}\times7^{1000}$ is $\boxed{7}$.

A continuous-time system that is initially at rest is described by

$${{dy(t)} \over {dt}} + 3y(t) = 2x(t)$$,

where $$x(t)$$ is the input voltage and $$y(t)$$ is the output voltage. The impulse response of the system is
en.explanation:
The continuous-time system is described by the differential equation:

$$\frac{dy(t)}{dt} + 3y(t) = 2x(t)$$

To find the impulse response of the system, we need to solve this equation for the case when the input voltage $$x(t)$$ is an impulse function, $$\delta(t)$$. An impulse function has the property that it is zero everywhere except at $ t = 0 $, where it is infinitely large in such a way to have a unit area.

So, we let $$x(t) = \delta(t)$$ and solve the differential equation:

$$\frac{dy(t)}{dt} + 3y(t) = 2\delta(t)$$

Take the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation. Recall that the Laplace transform of an impulse function $$\delta(t)$$ is 1. Also, we need to consider the initial condition, which is given as the system being initially at rest (this means $$y(0) = 0$$).

$$\mathcal{L}\left\{\frac{dy(t)}{dt}\right\} + \mathcal{L} \left\{3y(t)\right\} = \mathcal{L}\{2\delta(t)\}$$

Using the linear properties of the Laplace transform and the initial condition:

$$sY(s) - y(0) + 3Y(s) = 2$$

$$sY(s) + 3Y(s) = 2$$

$$Y(s)(s + 3) = 2$$

$$Y(s) = \frac{2}{s + 3}$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform to get the impulse response $$h(t)$$:

$$h(t) = 2e^{-3t}u(t)$$

Therefore, the impulse response of the system is:

Option C: $$2e^{-3t}u(t)$$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

The discrete-time Fourier transform of a signal $$x[n]$$ is $$X(\Omega ) = (1 + \cos \Omega ){e^{ - j\Omega }}$$. Consider that $${x_p}[n]$$ is a periodic signal of period N = 5 such that

$${x_p}[n] = x[n]$$, for $$n = 0,1,2$$

= 0, for $$n = 3,4$$

Note that $${x_p}[n] = \sum\nolimits\limits_{k = 0}^{n - 1} {{a_k}{e^{j{{2\pi } \over N}kn}}} $$. The magnitude of the Fourier series coeffiient $$a_3$$ is __________ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
en.explanation:
We know that, $a_k=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n) e^{\frac{-j 2 \pi}{N} k n}$

$$ \begin{aligned} & a_k=\left.\frac{1}{N} X(\Omega)\right|_{\Omega=\frac{2 \pi k}{N}} \\ & a_k=\left.\frac{1}{N}(1+\cos \Omega) e^{-j \Omega}\right|_{\Omega=\frac{2 \pi k}{N}}=\frac{1}{N}\left(1+\cos \frac{2 \pi k}{N}\right) e^{\frac{-j 2 \pi k}{N}} \\ & a_3=\frac{1}{5}\left(1+\cos \frac{2 \pi \times 3}{5}\right) e^{\frac{-j 2 \pi \times 3}{5}} \\ & a_3=\frac{1}{5}\left(1+\cos \frac{6 \pi}{5}\right) e^{\frac{-j 6 \pi}{5}} \\ & \left|a_3\right|=\frac{1}{5}\left(1+\cos \frac{6 \pi}{5}\right)=0.038 \end{aligned} $$

Frequency components present at sampler output,
